crm_note.how_it_went: Lukas described the round as mixed. He felt the first half (lock-free ring buffer) went well and was unsure about the second half (order book), where he ran out of time and the cancel path had a bug. He said Ellie told him they do not expect people to finish and want to see how a candidate moves off the naive version.

rounds.format: 90 minutes, shared editor, C++20, with two engineers from the execution tech team, Raj and Ellie. No compiler at first, then a compiler was turned on for the second half.
asked: Write a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer
Memory ordering choices, and why not seq_cst everywhere (Ellie)
False sharing: what happens if head and tail share a cache line
Order book with add, modify, cancel and fast best bid and ask
How to measure latency and know a change made things faster
Whether he had used kernel bypass
Virtual functions versus templates on the hot path
rounds.candidate_view: Lukas said the first half was really good and he is unsure about the second. He answered the ring buffer with atomic head and tail, power of two size with masking, release on the tail store, acquire on the other side's load and relaxed for a thread reading its own index. On false sharing he talked about padding to 64 bytes with alignas, and more on some chips because of the adjacent line prefetcher. In the order book he started with std::map, Raj asked what that does to the cache, and he then described a flat array indexed by price tick with a bitmap to find the best level. He ran out of time, the code compiled but the cancel path had a bug. For latency he said rdtsc, pinned cores, warm versus cold cache, and looking at the tail (99.9th percentile) rather than the mean. He has used kernel bypass on the market data side. On virtual functions versus templates he answered CRTP and gave his reasons. He said he is annoyed with himself about the second half.

candidate.subject: Brackenvane first round: next steps
candidate.body:
Hi Lukas,

Thanks for talking me through the coding round today. I'm glad the ring buffer section went the way you wanted, and Ellie's comment about how they look at the order book task is worth keeping in mind.

As agreed, the next steps are:
- I will ask Brackenvane for their feedback and confirm timing for the next round, which they said would be system design (a market data handler end to end) followed by a conversation with the head of the team. They said they move fast, maybe a week.
- I will let you know as soon as I hear.
- I will find out what I can about hours, and you can raise it with the head of team at the next round.

Speak soon.

Tom

process.round: First round: coding round (call dated 12 Nov 2026)
process.format: 90 minutes in a shared editor in C++20. There was no compiler at first, as the interviewers wanted to see you write. A compiler was turned on for the second half.
process.who: Two engineers from the execution tech team, Raj and Ellie.
process.what_they_look_for: Lock-free and cache-aware C++ on the hot path, and how you move off a naive first version. Ellie said they do not expect people to finish the order book task and want to see how you move off the naive version.

process.format: Design a market data handler end to end. This was described by the interviewers at the first round, so details beyond that are not discussed.

process.round: Round after that: chat with the head of the team
process.format: A conversation. Further detail not discussed.

question_themes.theme: Lock-free data structures and memory ordering
examples: Write a single-producer single-consumer lock-free ring buffer.
Which memory orderings would you use, and why not seq_cst everywhere?
What happens if head and tail sit on the same cache line?
Raj asked what a std::map does to your cache when it was used for the order book.
Handle add, modify and cancel on price levels and get the best bid and ask quickly.
Moving from std::map to a flat array indexed by price tick with a bitmap to find the best level.
How would you know a change made things faster?
Whether you have used kernel bypass.

question_themes.theme: Virtual functions versus templates on the hot path
examples: One question on virtual functions versus templates on the hot path, and the reasoning behind the choice.

went_well: The ring buffer task went well: atomic head and tail, a power of two size so you mask instead of using modulo, and acquire/release/relaxed ordering with a clear reason for avoiding seq_cst on the hot path.
The false sharing answer covered padding to 64 bytes with alignas, and padding more on some chips because of the adjacent line prefetcher. Raj wrote this down.
The latency measurement answer covered rdtsc, pinned cores, warm versus cold cache, and looking at the 99.9th percentile rather than the mean.
The virtual functions versus templates question was answered with CRTP and the reasons for it.
tripped_people_up: Starting the order book with std::map drew an immediate question from Raj about the effect on the cache.
The flat array with a bitmap design was not working by the end of the time. It compiled but the cancel path had a bug.
advice: Be ready to write a lock-free SPSC ring buffer from scratch in C++20 without a compiler, and to justify each memory order you choose.
Prepare to explain false sharing, cache line padding and alignas, including why you might pad more than 64 bytes on some chips.

For the order book, start with a cache-friendly layout such as a flat array indexed by price tick with a bitmap for the best level, rather than std::map. Practise getting the cancel path right within the time.
If you do not finish, talk through how you would move off the naive version, since the interviewers said that is what they want to see.
Prepare a clear answer on latency measurement, including tail percentiles, core pinning and warm versus cold cache, and be ready to say whether you have used kernel bypass.
Look ahead to the system design round on an end-to-end market data handler.
